title: Stripe evals: Measuring real-world coding agent performance
content:
Integration choices affect how much value a business gets from Stripe. Choosing current integration patterns helps businesses access new capabilities with less custom code and can reduce future migration work. Building an integration well also means handling payment failures, subscription changes, and webhook events.
As developers build with coding agents, we have observed that agents bias towards older APIs that are more prevalent in their pretraining corpus, miss key features, and hallucinate. Existing coding benchmarks don't catch this: they check whether the code passes deterministic checks, not whether the API integration is correct. We want developers building with agents to start on the best Stripe setup, and that begins with seeing where agents fall short today. So we built Stripe evals to measure that, and to identify ways to steer agents toward better integrations, through capabilities like the Stripe agent plugin.
Stripe evals measure how well coding agents build high-quality integrations given realistic, well-specified scenarios driven by a roleplaying agent. We ran 69 scenarios across one-time payments, subscriptions, and Connect (marketplaces and platforms), on 14 model and harness pairs, both with and without the Stripe agent plugin. The scenarios include tasks such as building a hosted checkout, implementing metered billing, managing per-seat subscriptions, and splitting marketplace payments.
The plugin helps. All 14 coding agents scored higher with it, by roughly 3 to 8 percentage points, and web searches fell 96% as models relied on trusted guidance. Models also behave differently from one another: Fable 5.1 made 53% more tool calls with the plugin, while Gemini 3.8 Flash made 26% fewer. While the headline numbers are high, a strict pass rate requiring all necessary criteria to pass drops the average score across all agents from 78.1% to 29.4%.
We are also publishing our Stripe benchmark and eval framework. We will maintain the eval harness and update the results on an ongoing basis with new models, cases, and features.
Detailed results
The results below evaluate the coding agents on our 69 public cases (19 Connect, 24 payments, and 26 Subscriptions) over 2 runs.
Table 1: Detailed score results
*This is an aggregation across the Payments, Connect, and Subscriptions cases, which have differing model performance, and so cross-model comparisons should be contextualized with Table 3.
Plugin helps model performance
In our evals, all 14 model and harness pairs scored higher with the plugin, improving by roughly 3 to 8 percentage points overall. The plugin also helped reduce outdated parameter references from 7% to 1.3% of the parameters in API calls. For example, without the plugin GPT 6.1 Sol on the payments-mobile-physical-goods scenario used a recently removed parameter payment_method_types: ['card'], but with the plugin the model writes the correct automatic_payment_methods: { enabled: true }, enabling Dynamic Payment Methods.
Test volume decrease from the plugin
With the plugin, coding agents wrote about 40% fewer test lines and ran tests in 42% of evals vs 53% without the plugin. This doesn’t mean fewer tests improved performance, but rather more authoritative information from the plugin reduced the need for excessive checking of written code.
Table 2: Tool calls
*OpenCode used web search via OpenRouter, which we cannot directly observe.
Agents replace web search for the plugin
The plugin includes MCP tool calls (such as doc search, implementation planner) and skills. Generally, the plugin reduces the need for about 1.2 web searches per eval. Web fetches (the way agents pull web content from a URL) also decrease by about 3 fetches per eval.
Yet not every model behaves the same. Interestingly, Argon and Grok fetch more when they’re using the plugin. They tend to fetch particular pages referenced in tool results or in skills.
Strict grading drastically reduces evaluation metrics
To measure if an integration satisfies all key requirements for good quality, we also report the strict pass rate for the required criteria (details in the scoring and reporting section below). In this reporting, the average model performance drops precipitously from 78.1% to 29.4% for the same required criteria. This indicates many of the models create almost correct implementations and have difficulty with the last mile. For example, in the payments-radar-review-fulfillment scenario, Opus 5.5 doesn’t check whether an order is eligible for fulfillment, only PaymentIntent.status === 'succeeded', which can allow orders to ship after refund or dispute.
Table 3: Scenario categories
*There were significant differences in agent performance across the scenario categories: one-time payments, subscriptions, and Connect. Coding agents that scored higher in one-time payments and subscriptions did not score the highest for Connect. Connect scenarios that involved more scenario-specific integration decisions also saw a larger gain from the use of plugins compared to the other categories.
Methodology
Coding agents
We chose three coding harnesses: Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and a sampling of models including open-weight models.
Stripe agent plugin
The Stripe agent plugin gives coding agents Stripe-authored skills and access to tools through our Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Skills provide integration best practices, while tools such as stripe_implementation_planner and search_stripe_documentation supply implementation guidance and current documentation. API search and details tools help agents look up supported operations and parameters.
Web search
To best simulate the developer experience, we provided the most native web search available to the coding harness. For all Claude Code models and Codex models we used the web search the harnesses provide. For OpenCode, we used the OpenRouter Web Search server tool, which tries to use native provider search if available or falls back to Exa.
Using an LLM to proxy a human with latent needs
Developers typically start with a goal, not complete requirements, and guide coding agents through iterative feedback and key decisions. To evaluate these interactions, we use a secondary agent to role-play the developer without teaching the coding agent how to pass the benchmark.
The roleplayer is instructed to steer the coding agent towards the desired product outcome but not assume expertise in Stripe APIs. It asks the coding agent to investigate and make all integration decisions. It is also instructed not to write code, echo the agent’s answer, or expand into generic application concerns.
Just as a human developer has a latent set of needs when coming to the coding agent, our roleplayer derives a frozen, private set of needs from the initial prompt and context prior to the conversation. For example, a user building a platform that charges a flat $0.50 per payment may want to understand the unit economics even if not asked upfront. At the end of each turn, the roleplaying agent decides if all the needs are met. The roleplaying agent normally identifies two to four needs, with a maximum of six. On each turn, the roleplayer selects one unresolved need and turns it into a follow-up question. It never exposes the complete list.
The roleplayer agent only stops during normal operation when no needs remain or if a preset limit on turns is reached. This keeps the agent on track like a focused developer would be, yet allows for natural flexibility if a small detour is required for the completion of the task. The harness records the needs and their progression for auditability, but that private state is never sent to the coding agent or the judges.
Evaluating agents in a realistic loop
Coding agents were run headlessly in an isolated workspace with access to their normal coding tools and web search. They could inspect the repository, write files, run commands, and revise their implementation over multiple turns interacting with the role

report.summary: Stripe built a 69-scenario benchmark showing coding agents often build outdated or incomplete Stripe integrations, but its agent plugin improves scores by 3–8 points.
report.background: Coding agents are increasingly used to build payment integrations, but they tend to favor older APIs that are more common in their pretraining data, miss important features, and hallucinate. Existing coding benchmarks mostly check whether generated code passes deterministic tests, not whether an API integration is correct, secure, or maintainable. Stripe integrations are also complex: developers must handle payment failures, subscription changes, webhook events, and marketplace payment splits. A flawed integration can cost businesses money or require painful migrations later. Stripe therefore built an evaluation framework to measure how well coding agents handle realistic integration tasks, identify where they fall short, and test whether authoritative guidance such as the Stripe agent plugin can steer them toward current best practices.
key_points: Stripe evaluated 14 model and harness pairs on 69 public scenarios: 24 one-time payments, 26 subscriptions, and 19 Connect cases. A roleplaying agent simulated a developer with hidden needs, asking follow-up questions without revealing the full requirements. Each scenario ran twice in an isolated workspace, letting agents inspect code, write files, run commands, and revise over multiple turns.

The Stripe agent plugin improved all 14 model and harness pairs by roughly 3 to 8 percentage points. It also cut outdated parameter references from 7% to 1.3% of API-call parameters. For example, one model switched from a removed payment_method_types parameter to the correct automatic_payment_methods setting, enabling Dynamic Payment Methods.

Strict grading reveals a last-mile problem. When every required criterion must pass, average scores fall from 78.1% to 29.4%. In one example, Opus 5.5 checked only whether a PaymentIntent succeeded, not whether an order was eligible for fulfillment, potentially allowing shipments after refunds or disputes.

Agent behavior varies widely. With the plugin, Fable 5.1 made 53% more tool calls while Gemini 3.8 Flash made 26% fewer. Web searches fell 96%, about 1.2 fewer searches per eval, and web fetches dropped by about 3 per eval. Agents also wrote roughly 40% fewer test lines and ran tests in 42% of evals versus 53% without the plugin.

Performance differs by scenario category. Agents that scored highest on one-time payments and subscriptions did not necessarily lead on Connect. Connect scenarios involving more integration-specific decisions saw larger gains from the plugin, suggesting authoritative guidance matters most when tasks require nuanced platform or marketplace choices.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Stripe’s evals push agent benchmarks beyond deterministic code checks toward realistic, multi-turn API correctness. The results show that context and tooling—such as MCP servers, skills, and current documentation—can materially reduce hallucination and outdated API usage. For developers, the plugin can improve integration quality, but the strict pass-rate collapse shows agents still struggle with the final requirements: edge cases, compliance, and business logic. Teams should treat agent output as a draft requiring review, testing, and guardrails. For regular users and businesses, better agent-built Stripe setups could mean fewer failed payments, smoother subscriptions, and less migration work—but subtly wrong payment logic remains a real risk if teams ship without verification.
report.tools: Watch the Stripe agent plugin and its MCP server, especially tools like stripe_implementation_planner, search_stripe_documentation, and API search/details. Stripe plans to publish its benchmark and eval framework, so follow that repository for new cases and model results. The evals used Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode harnesses, with OpenRouter web search and Exa as search fallbacks. Developers can use these to compare agent performance and test plugin-enabled workflows.
